job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work from a shared office in Lille, in a startup of eleven people that builds route-planning software for delivery firms. I'm the junior developer, so I fix small bugs, write tests and ask my AI assistant for the first draft of almost everything. I studied computer science and passed, nothing flashy, no internship, because I spent those summers working in a bike shop. I share a flat with two friends near the Vieux-Lille market, and in the evenings I'm usually on a side project.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the side project, and how did you get this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a small app that tells cyclists which streets have broken bike lanes, built from open city data. Nobody pays for it yet, but it taught me more than half my degree. I got the job because the founder, Odile, saw the app and said she'd rather hire someone who builds things. My parents are fine with money, my dad teaches and my mum runs a pharmacy, so I've got a cushion, and I've never felt I had to take the first thing offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools are handy and the headlines are overheated. At work I'd tell Odile it saves me a couple of hours a week and nobody should rebuild the company around it. Online I'd probably joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fine. I'd keep my edge anyway, because the junior who knows the tools well gets trusted faster. The one thing I'd resent is bosses using the word AI to justify low pay rises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep the assistant in my daily routine and spend the evenings on my cycling app. I'd save about 500 euros a month toward a deposit, and I'd join the tech-workers' collective that meets in a bar on Thursdays. I'm also thinking about asking for a pay review at the six-month mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I prepared for and it's kind to me. I'd feel a small itch that nothing is changing fast enough to be interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. If it turns out to be hype, what happens to your habits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get bored and try another stack. If the tools stall, I'd learn a lower-level language like Rust, just for the fun and the CV. Being adaptable means I need something new to chew on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the money. Rents in Lille keep climbing and my room costs nearly 40 percent of my pay. I'm fine because my parents would help, but it's a real pressure for people who don't have that.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy** and the headlines are overheated.
I'd tell Odile (my boss) nobody should rebuild the company around it.
think: The junior who knows the tools well gets **trusted** faster, and I'm that junior.
I'd resent bosses using AI to justify low **pay** rises.
do: Keep using the assistant daily and work on the **cycling app**.
Save **500 euros** a month toward a deposit.
Join the tech-workers' **collective** and ask for a pay review at six months.
feel: **Calm**, with an itch that nothing changes fast enough to be interesting.
S0.quote: I'd keep my edge anyway, because the junior who knows the tools well gets trusted faster.
fieldNote: Already **fluent** with AI, so a quiet world costs him nothing.
His one grievance is **pay** and rent, not job loss.
Rent takes about 40 percent of his pay, which his parents' backing hides.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for first drafts every day
Save 500 euros a month toward a flat deposit
Join the Thursday tech-workers' collective
Ask Odile for a pay review at six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening, so let's make it fair. I'd say the gains from AI should be shared, with a shorter week or higher pay, not used to hire fewer juniors. I'd also say that publicly, because people my age are watching their entry jobs get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd see it as an opportunity with a trap. Coding is exactly the thinking task that gets taken first, so a junior who only writes code is in danger. A junior who understands the delivery business and directs the tools is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from writing code to specifying and checking it, and spend time with Odile's customers, the dispatchers, to learn what they need. I'd turn the cycling app into something I can sell to councils, as a side income. I'd keep up the collective, too, since someone must push on pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in an energised way. I'm in the line of fire, but I'm also near the front of it, which is a decent place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which skills would you bet on if software takes over the building itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bet on knowing a domain, like logistics, plus being the person who can say whether the AI's work is right. I'd also learn how to talk to customers, because tools can't sit in a room and read someone's face yet. Those skills are the safest ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean my cousin Lucas, who is a junior accountant. He's not adaptive, and he'd be hurt first. I'd show him the tools on a Sunday and try to talk him into practising.

People my age are watching entry-level jobs get **cut**, and I'd say so publicly.

feel: **Uneasy** but energised, since I'm in the line of fire and near the front.

fieldNote: He turns exposure into a **plan** quickly, typical of an adaptive worker.

Mixes fairness politics with practical self-positioning.

steps.text: Shift from writing code to writing specs and reviewing output
Spend one afternoon a week with Odile's dispatcher customers
Pitch the cycling app to two local councils
Keep going to the tech-workers' collective on Thursdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to be ready, and we need emergency measures: a basic income, retraining that's actually paid, and rules on companies firing people for AI. I'd say that in public, on the street if I had to. I'd also say it to Odile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2028 almost every junior developer job disappears, mine included. Robots come around 2031, so the hands-on world stays for a bit longer. I'm adaptive, but there's a limit to how fast you can move when everyone's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd put all my savings into a separate account and stop paying for anything I don't need. I'd talk to my dad about whether a pharmacy or school job could be a fallback, since those need humans and trust. I'd also try to make the cycling app earn something so I have my own thing. And I'd join a protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not paralysed, I'm moving, but I'm frightened that the whole ladder disappears before I'm halfway up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Odile what you were planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd tell Odile. She's honest with us and I'd rather she hear it from me. If she's cutting, I'd offer to take fewer hours or a lower pay if it kept a colleague on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try to learn that code can't replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell her I want to learn how the firm's customers think. If the code goes, relationships stay for a while. That may sound cold, but it's survival.

say: It's too fast for anyone to be ready, so we need **emergency** measures like a basic income.
I'd say it to Odile and, if needed, in the **street**.
think: By 2028 almost every junior developer job disappears, **mine** included.
I'm adaptive, but there's a **limit** to how fast you can move when everyone's moving.

feel: **Anxious**: I'm moving, but frightened the whole ladder vanishes before I'm halfway up.
S2.quote: I'm frightened that the whole ladder disappears before I'm halfway up.
fieldNote: Offers to take fewer hours to keep a colleague, which shows his **values**.
Looks for human-trust work like pharmacy or schools as a fallback.

steps.text: Move my savings into a separate emergency account
Cancel subscriptions and cut eating out
Make the cycling app charge councils a small fee
Ask my parents about a pharmacy or school job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to prepare properly, so let's use it. I'd say we need new rules about who owns the gains, and training funded by the companies. I'd tell friends to build a skill that's about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel okay. By 2031 I could run my own tiny company or be in a role that's all customer work and judgement. That's the better version of my life. The worst version is the one where I wait and then rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a real business on the cycling app and try to get two or three paying city councils within two years. I'd stay at my job and use the assistant for everything, but start a part-time degree in urban planning. Planning needs people, laws and local knowledge, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Five years is enough to do something with, which is a very different feeling from two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask politicians for in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a shorter working week with the same pay, funded by company profits. I'd also ask for tax on firms that replace large numbers of workers. And I'd ask for a free retraining place that doesn't bury people in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you worried about in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried about some of my friends. I know two who are not adaptive and are putting off every plan. I'd help them, but I can't carry them.

I'd tell friends to build a skill that's about **people**.
think: By 2031 I could run a tiny **company** or be in a role that's all customer work and judgement.
The worst version of my life is the one where I wait and then **rush**.

feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, because five years is enough to do something with.

fieldNote: Calls out friends who put off plans, showing the **adaptability** gap he sees.

steps.text: Sign two city councils as paying users of the cycling app
Enrol in a part-time urban planning degree
Use the AI assistant for tests, drafts and reviews
Write to my local councillor about shared AI gains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best-case timeline if we act. I'd push for public ownership of some of the gains, a robot tax maybe, and pilot programmes for shorter weeks. I'd tell friends to enjoy their twenties but not ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty calm. I'm 22, and at 32 I'll still be adaptable. I'd say the main risk is that people get complacent in years three to eight, and then the last two arrive as a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for three years, learn everything I can, then try a start-up of my own in urban data. I'd keep saving, and put money into a diverse fund. I'd also try to build a small circle of people who help each other find work when things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. A decade is a lot of time to build something that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you build, and what would you not do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy a car or a house in a hurry, since both might change. I'd rent, save, and keep my options wide. Staying light is a good tactic for the next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that I'm fine, I'm saving, and they shouldn't worry about me. They'd probably say it's their job to worry. I'd say they can worry about my sister, who is still at school and will be the one who really lives through this.

I'd tell friends to enjoy their twenties but not **ignore** it.
think: At 32 I'll still be **adaptable**, so I feel calm.
The main risk is **complacency** in years three to eight, then the last two arrive as a shock.

fieldNote: Calm comes from **adaptability** and money, not from believing the risk is small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Even with my good start, two years is too short for the world to change its rules. What would help is a basic income, paid retraining and a rule that firms must give notice before replacing people with AI. I'd also want a community of people to lean on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that being adaptive isn't the same as being safe. People tell me I'll be fine because I like the tools. I'd rather the system were fine for everyone.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive isn't the same as being safe.
portrait: Ben is **22**, a junior developer at an eleven-person logistics software startup in Lille, with a pass degree and no internship.
He uses AI every day, builds a **cycling app** on the side and has strong savings and family backing.
He leans left and wants shared gains, shorter weeks, **notice** rules and a tech-workers' collective.
He moves fast in every scenario, ranging from calm to **anxious**, and worries most about friends who delay.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is too short for the world to change its **rules**.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income, paid **retraining**, notice before AI replacement and a community to lean on.
